summary: We are testing whether a 'break-and-extend' technique for very sparse directed graphs (avg degree < 4) can improve the overall judge score from 82 to 83 by specifically improving test 10's path length past the ~23,333 vertex threshold. The prior two iterations established a baseline of 82/100 using SCC-based ordering plus Pósa rotation, but test 10 (a sparse graph) stalls at ~21,000 vertices because rotation only works at the path tail.
key_points: Main arm (h-main): Adds a new solveBreakExtend() function that truncates the path back to the nearest 'escape vertex' (one with an unvisited out-neighbor), redirects through it, and re-extends greedily — run as multi-restart (0.2s/attempt, ~15 attempts in 3.1s). Predicts score rises from 82→83, with test 10's k increasing from ~21,000 to ~25,000.
Control arm (h-control-negative): Runs the unchanged iter-2 solution to confirm the 82-point baseline still holds, isolating any score improvement to the break-and-extend mechanism specifically.

Confirmation criteria: Score of 83 on h-main AND 82 on h-control confirms the hypothesis. If h-main scores 82 or lower, break-and-extend failed to cross the test-10 threshold — diagnostics include checking the actual k value on test 10 and whether the avg_deg < 4 branching condition fires correctly. Regression on tests 1-9 would indicate the branching condition is misclassifying dense graphs as sparse.

Design is well-scoped: single new mechanism targeting a single test case, with clear pass/fail criteria and specified diagnostics. The 0.2s per-attempt budget was empirically tuned, and escape vertex search is bounded at 100 positions from the tail.
